Rosa had wanted to paint the library mural since the first day of fifth grade, so when Ms. Patel announced that two students would design it together, Rosa raised her hand so quickly that her elbow cracked.

Her partner turned out to be Ethan Brooks, a quiet boy who decorated every scrap of paper with dragons. Rosa preferred to draw flowers, tropical birds, and the colorful outdoor market where her grandmother sold mangoes.

At their first meeting, Ethan unrolled an enormous sketch of a green dragon curling across the entire page and breathing fire over a castle. "This goes in the middle," he declared. "It's going to be incredible."

Rosa frowned. "It's a library, not a battlefield, and the kindergarteners will be terrified."

"Little kids love dragons," Ethan snapped. "Your flowers are boring."

The word stung like a bee. Rosa grabbed her pencil case and stood up, determined to march straight to Ms. Patel and ask for a new partner. Then she remembered something her grandmother always said: a closed fist cannot shake hands.

She sat back down. "Okay," she said slowly. "Tell me why the dragon matters so much to you."

Ethan looked surprised, and he picked nervously at the corner of his sketch. "My dad reads me dragon stories every night," he admitted. "They're the reason I actually enjoy reading."

Rosa considered that before she pulled out her own drawing. "My grandmother taught me to read using the signs at the market," she explained. "That's why every flower here has a word written beside it."

For a long moment, neither of them spoke. Then Ethan pointed at her page. "What if the dragon is flying over your market, and instead of fire, he's breathing out letters and words?"

Rosa felt a smile tug at her mouth. "And the words could transform into flowers when they land."

They worked through lunch for the rest of the week, with Ethan painting the shimmering scales while Rosa painted the market stalls and the swirling words. They still disagreed about colors, but now their arguments ended in laughter instead of slammed doors.

On the afternoon the mural was finished, a first grader stood in front of it for ten minutes, sounding out every word the dragon had breathed. Rosa and Ethan watched from the doorway, and neither of them said "I told you so." There was nothing left to win.
stem: Which sentence best states a theme of the story?
choices: Listening to someone else's reasons can turn a conflict into something better for everyone.
Younger students should always be the ones who choose the art in a library.
Talented artists do their best work when they are allowed to work alone.
The best way to keep a friendship is to win every argument.
explanation: Rosa almost quits, but when she asks Ethan why the dragon matters, they discover a shared love of reading and create a mural better than either plan. The story never says artists should work alone, never lets young students choose, and the ending says there was 'nothing left to win.'

Hannah Pratt was eleven years old in the spring of 1769, and she disliked the spinning wheel more than any other chore. It squeaked, the wool tangled, and her thread always came out lumpy. Her older sister, Abigail, could spin a smooth strand while humming a hymn, but Hannah could barely spin while holding her breath.

"Why can't we just buy cloth from the shop the way we used to?" Hannah grumbled one morning.

Mother set down her basket. "Because that cloth comes from England, and the British government has placed new taxes on many goods it sends to the colonies. Your father and the other men in town have promised not to purchase British goods until the taxes are removed. If we want new clothes, we must make them ourselves."

Hannah knew about the taxes, since everyone in town discussed them. Still, it seemed unfair that a king across the ocean could decide how she spent her mornings.

That afternoon, Abigail rushed in with news. "The minister's wife is organizing a spinning bee on Saturday," she announced. "Girls from all over town will spin together on the green to demonstrate that we can make our own cloth."

Hannah's stomach dropped. Spinning in front of the entire town would be far worse than spinning alone, because everyone would notice her lumpy thread.

For the next three evenings, Abigail sat beside her near the fire. She showed Hannah how to keep her foot steady on the pedal and how to let the wool slip gently through her fingers instead of squeezing it. Gradually, the lumps grew smaller and the thread grew smoother.

On Saturday, the green was crowded with wheels, and their steady whirring sounded like a hive full of bees. Hannah finally understood the name. Neighbors brought bread and cider, and an elderly farmer in a patched coat wandered from wheel to wheel, nodding with approval.

When he reached Hannah, she froze. He picked up the end of her thread and rolled it between his fingers. "Not perfect," he said, "but strong. Every strand helps, young lady."

By sunset, her arms ached, and Hannah's thread still had a few bumps. Yet when she looked across the green at the long rows of wheels, she felt something unexpected: pride. The squeaky wheel was no longer just a chore; it was her way of standing up for her community.
stem: What is the main reason the town holds the spinning bee?
choices: to teach young girls how to bake bread and make cider
to raise money so the town can pay the new British taxes
to show that the colonists can make their own cloth instead of buying British goods
to choose which girl is the best spinner in town
explanation: Abigail says the girls 'will spin together on the green to demonstrate that we can make our own cloth.' This connects to the town's promise not to buy British goods while the taxes remain.

On Habitat Seven, the only green things for a million miles grew inside the greenhouse dome. Twelve-year-old Kai Mendoza had volunteered there every morning since his family moved to the moon, and he loved the earthy smell of damp soil, which was the only thing that reminded him of home.

So when the emergency alarm began to wail during breakfast, Kai dropped his spoon and raced down the corridor.

Inside the dome, the air felt thin and frigid. Rows of bean plants were drooping like exhausted soldiers, and a small maintenance robot named Pip rolled toward him with its blue light blinking rapidly.

"Heater failure in Section B," Pip announced. "Temperature is falling. Plants will freeze in approximately forty minutes."

"Where's Dr. Osei?" Kai asked.

"Dr. Osei is outside repairing the solar panels. She will not return for two hours."

Kai's heart pounded like a drum. He was not permitted to touch the heater, and the rule was printed in enormous red letters across the control panel: AUTHORIZED ADULTS ONLY.

He pressed the radio button. "Dr. Osei, the greenhouse heater is broken! What should I do?"

Only static answered, because the solar panels were located on the far side of the crater, out of range.

Kai studied the drooping plants. Those beans were not merely plants; they were dinner for forty people next month. He considered breaking the rule, and then he considered another possibility.

"Pip," he said, "the plants need heat, not necessarily the heater. What else in here produces heat?"

Pip's light flickered while it searched its files. "Grow lamps produce heat. Section A lamps are currently off for the night cycle."

Kai grinned, because switching on grow lamps was one of his regular daily responsibilities. Together, he and Pip dragged the tall lamp stands from Section A into Section B and switched them on, and warm orange light spilled across the leaves.

Kai watched the thermometer anxiously. For ten long minutes, the number barely moved, but then it crept upward one degree, then two.

When Dr. Osei finally hurried through the airlock, she discovered Kai asleep against a lamp stand, with Pip parked beside him like a loyal dog. Every bean plant was standing tall.

She read the computer log, then knelt beside him. "You followed the rule and rescued the crop," she said quietly. "That is harder than accomplishing only one of those things."
stem: What is the main problem Kai faces in the story?
choices: He must convince his family to move back to Earth.
He must repair the solar panels before Dr. Osei returns.
He must save the freezing plants without breaking the rule about the heater.
He must find Pip, who has rolled away during the alarm.
explanation: The heater fails and the plants will freeze in forty minutes, but only adults may touch the heater and Dr. Osei cannot be reached. Kai has to protect the crop while still following the rule.

Pour a spoonful of sugar into a glass of warm water and stir. In a few seconds, the white grains seem to vanish. The water looks exactly as clear as it did before. Has the sugar disappeared? Scientists would say no, and they can prove it.

Everything around you is made of matter. Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Your desk, the air you breathe, and the water in your glass are all matter. Matter is built from particles that are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.

When sugar dissolves, its particles spread out evenly among the water particles. The sugar is still there, but the pieces are now too tiny and too scattered for your eyes to notice. A mixture like this, in which one substance spreads evenly through another, is called a solution.

One simple test shows that the sugar is still present. Take a small sip. The water now tastes sweet, so the sugar has not gone anywhere. Another test uses a scale. Weigh a cup of water and a spoonful of sugar separately, and add the two numbers. Next, stir the sugar into the water and weigh the mixture. The total weight stays the same. Even though the sugar can no longer be seen, every particle is still counted.

Scientists call this idea conservation of matter. It means that when substances mix, melt, freeze, or dissolve, the total amount of matter stays the same. Particles can move around and change position, but they do not simply vanish.

You can even get the sugar back. If you leave the sugar water in a sunny window for several days, the water will slowly evaporate into the air. As the water leaves, the sugar particles crowd closer together. Eventually, small crystals form on the bottom of the glass. The sugar was there the whole time, waiting.

Not every substance dissolves, however. Stir sand into water, and the grains will sink to the bottom. Sand and water make a mixture, but not a solution, because the sand does not spread out evenly.

So the next time something seems to disappear, think like a scientist. Ask yourself where its particles went. Chances are, the matter is still nearby, just hidden from view.

In December of 1777, the American Revolution was not going well for the Continental Army. British soldiers had captured Philadelphia, the largest city in the colonies. General George Washington needed a safe place for his tired troops to spend the winter. He chose Valley Forge, a windy area of hills about twenty miles from the city.

When the army marched in on December 19, about twelve thousand soldiers arrived. Many had no shoes. Some left bloody footprints in the snow. Their first job was to build shelter. Working in small groups, the men cut down trees and built wooden huts. Each hut was about fourteen feet long and held twelve soldiers. Within a few weeks, a small city of logs stood on the frozen hills.

The huts kept out the wind, but they could not solve every problem. Food and clothing were hard to find. Farmers often preferred to sell their crops to the British, who paid in silver coins instead of paper money. On some days, soldiers ate only firecake, a plain mix of flour and water baked on hot stones. Even worse, diseases spread quickly through the crowded camp. About two thousand soldiers died that winter, mostly from illness rather than cold.

Then, in February of 1778, help arrived in an unusual form. A Prussian officer named Baron Friedrich von Steuben came to camp. He spoke very little English, yet he knew a great deal about training an army. Steuben began drilling a small group of soldiers. He taught them to march in step, to load their muskets quickly, and to charge together. Those soldiers then taught others. Before long, the whole army was practicing the same skills.

The change was remarkable. The soldiers who had stumbled into Valley Forge in December marched out in June as a stronger, more confident army. Only days later, they fought the British at the Battle of Monmouth in New Jersey. The fight ended without a clear winner, but the Americans held their ground against well-trained British troops.

Today, many historians consider Valley Forge a turning point in the war. No major battle was fought there; instead, the army won a quieter victory. It survived a terrible winter and learned to fight as one.

Picture a schoolyard where students pull carrots from the ground, chase butterflies between rows of sunflowers, and taste a tomato still warm from the sun. I believe every elementary school in the United States should have a garden like this. A school garden costs very little, and it teaches lessons that no textbook can.

First, gardens make science come alive. In class, students read that plants need water, air, and light to grow. In a garden, they see it happen. When students forget to water their bean plants for a week, they watch the leaves droop and turn yellow. That lesson sticks far better than a page in a book. Gardens also show how living things depend on one another. Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, and worms loosen the soil so roots can spread.

Second, gardens help children eat better. Many kids refuse to touch vegetables at dinner. Yet something surprising happens when they grow the vegetables themselves. Teachers across the country report that students who plant and harvest lettuce are much more willing to eat a salad. Pride, it seems, is a powerful seasoning.

Third, gardens teach responsibility and teamwork. A garden cannot be finished in one afternoon. Someone must water it, pull weeds, and protect it from hungry rabbits. Students learn to make schedules, share jobs, and keep promises to one another. If one group slacks off, everyone can see the result.

Some people argue that schools do not have enough space or money for gardens. This concern is understandable, but it is not a good reason to give up. A garden does not need to be large. A few wooden boxes along a sunny wall can grow herbs, peppers, and strawberries. Many local hardware stores and garden clubs are happy to donate seeds, soil, and tools. Parents and grandparents often volunteer their time, too.

Others worry that gardening takes time away from reading and math. In fact, gardens can strengthen those subjects. Students measure how tall their plants grow, keep journals about what they observe, and calculate how many seeds fit in each row.

A school garden is more than a patch of dirt. It is a classroom without walls. Let's give every child the chance to dig in.

Picture a schoolyard where students pull carrots from the ground, chase butterflies between rows of sunflowers, and taste a tomato still warm from the sun. I believe every elementary school in the United States should have a garden like this. A school garden costs very little, and it teaches lessons that no textbook can.

First, gardens make science come alive. In class, students read that plants need water, air, and light to grow. In a garden, they see it happen. When students forget to water their bean plants for a week, they watch the leaves droop and turn yellow. That lesson sticks far better than a page in a book. Gardens also show how living things depend on one another. Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, and worms loosen the soil so roots can spread.

Second, gardens help children eat better. Many kids refuse to touch vegetables at dinner. Yet something surprising happens when they grow the vegetables themselves. Teachers across the country report that students who plant and harvest lettuce are much more willing to eat a salad. Pride, it seems, is a powerful seasoning.

Third, gardens teach responsibility and teamwork. A garden cannot be finished in one afternoon. Someone must water it, pull weeds, and protect it from hungry rabbits. Students learn to make schedules, share jobs, and keep promises to one another. If one group slacks off, everyone can see the result.

Some people argue that schools do not have enough space or money for gardens. This concern is understandable, but it is not a good reason to give up. A garden does not need to be large. A few wooden boxes along a sunny wall can grow herbs, peppers, and strawberries. Many local hardware stores and garden clubs are happy to donate seeds, soil, and tools. Parents and grandparents often volunteer their time, too.

Others worry that gardening takes time away from reading and math. In fact, gardens can strengthen those subjects. Students measure how tall their plants grow, keep journals about what they observe, and calculate how many seeds fit in each row.

A school garden is more than a patch of dirt. It is a classroom without walls. Let's give every child the chance to dig in.

stem: The words INSPECT, SPECTATOR, and SPECTACLES all share the root SPECT. What does SPECT most likely mean?
explanation: To inspect is to look closely, a spectator watches an event, and spectacles help people see. The Latin root spect means 'to look.'

stem: What does the prefix in MISUNDERSTAND mean?
explanation: The prefix mis- means 'wrongly' or 'badly.' To misunderstand is to understand something wrongly.

stem: Which phrase best explains the meaning of DEPENDABLE?
explanation: The suffix -able means 'able to be.' Dependable means able to be depended on, or trusted.

stem: The Greek root GRAPH appears in AUTOGRAPH, PARAGRAPH, and PHOTOGRAPH. What does GRAPH mean?
explanation: An autograph is a person's own written name, a paragraph is a section of writing, and a photograph is 'drawn' with light. Graph means 'write or draw.' (Auto means 'self,' phon means 'sound,' and tele means 'far.')

stem: TRANSPORT, PORTABLE, and EXPORT share the Latin root PORT. What does PORT mean?
explanation: To transport is to carry across, something portable can be carried, and exports are goods carried out of a country. Port means 'carry.'

stem: Which word is a SYNONYM for ENORMOUS?
explanation: Enormous means extremely large, so huge is a synonym. Tiny is an antonym.

stem: Which word is a SYNONYM for RELUCTANT?
explanation: A reluctant person does not want to do something. Unwilling has the same meaning; eager is the opposite.

stem: Which word is an ANTONYM for FRAGILE?
explanation: Fragile means easily broken. Sturdy means strong and hard to break, so it is the opposite. Delicate and breakable are synonyms.

stem: Which word is an ANTONYM for ANCIENT?
explanation: Ancient means very old, from long ago. Modern means new or of the present time, so it is the opposite.

stem: Read the sentence: "The desert is so ARID that it may not rain there for months." What does ARID mean?
explanation: The clue 'it may not rain there for months' shows that arid means very dry.

stem: Read the sentence: "After running the long race, Marcus was so EXHAUSTED that he fell asleep on the bus." What does EXHAUSTED mean?
explanation: Running a long race and then falling asleep are clues that exhausted means extremely tired.

stem: Read the sentence: "Before the experiment, Lena wrote her HYPOTHESIS: 'I think the plant in the sunny window will grow taller.'" What is a HYPOTHESIS?
choices: a prediction that can be tested
explanation: Lena writes 'I think...' before the experiment begins. A hypothesis is a prediction, or educated guess, that an experiment can test.

stem: In which sentence does WIND mean "to turn or twist something around"?
choices: Please WIND the yarn into a tight ball.
A cold WIND came down from the mountains.
We could hear the WIND whistling through the trees.
The WIND blew the leaves across the yard.
explanation: Only 'WIND the yarn into a ball' uses wind as a verb meaning to turn or twist. In the other sentences, wind is a noun meaning moving air.

stem: Read the sentence: "The principal will PRESENT the trophy at the assembly." What does PRESENT mean in this sentence?
explanation: Here present is a verb: the principal will give, or hand over, the trophy in a formal way. The other choices are different meanings of the same spelling.

stem: Read the sentence: "The nurse cleaned the WOUND on my knee and covered it with a bandage." What does WOUND mean?
explanation: A nurse cleans and bandages an injury, so wound means an injury in this sentence. 'Turned around something' is the meaning of wound (rhymes with sound), the past tense of wind.

stem: On the first day of camp, the counselor played a silly game to BREAK THE ICE. What does BREAK THE ICE mean?
choices: help people feel relaxed when they first meet
explanation: The idiom 'break the ice' means to do something that helps people feel comfortable when they first meet.

stem: "I have a spelling test tomorrow, so I need to HIT THE BOOKS tonight." What does HIT THE BOOKS mean?
explanation: The idiom 'hit the books' means to study. The clue is the spelling test the next day.

stem: Diego said the math quiz was A PIECE OF CAKE. What did he mean?
choices: The quiz was about fractions of a cake.
explanation: The idiom 'a piece of cake' means something is very easy to do.

stem: What is the meaning of the proverb DON'T COUNT YOUR CHICKENS BEFORE THEY HATCH?
choices: Don't depend on something good happening until it really happens.
Count carefully so that you do not make mistakes.
Be patient while you wait for spring to come.
Always take good care of animals on a farm.
explanation: Eggs might not all hatch, so counting chickens early is a mistake. The proverb warns not to rely on a result before it actually happens.

stem: What does the saying THE EARLY BIRD CATCHES THE WORM mean?
choices: Birds are hungriest early in the morning.
It is unwise to wake up before sunrise.
People should share what they find with others.
People who start early have a better chance of success.
explanation: The bird that wakes up first gets the worm. The saying means that people who act early get an advantage.

stem: What does the adage ACTIONS SPEAK LOUDER THAN WORDS mean?

What you do shows more about you than what you say.
People who talk a lot are usually very active.
It is better to stay quiet than to give an opinion.
explanation: The adage means that a person's actions prove what they really think or feel better than their words do.

stem: Complete the analogy. HOT is to COLD as TALL is to ______.
explanation: Hot and cold are opposites. The opposite of tall is short. High and large have meanings similar to tall, not opposite.

stem: Complete the analogy. PETAL is to FLOWER as PAGE is to ______.
explanation: A petal is one part of a flower, and a page is one part of a book. This is a part-to-whole relationship.

stem: Complete the analogy. AUTHOR is to NOVEL as COMPOSER is to ______.
explanation: An author creates a novel, and a composer creates a symphony. The relationship is creator to the thing created.

stem: Your teacher asks you to ANALYZE a poem. What should you do?

study its parts carefully to understand how it works

stem: When you SUMMARIZE a story, what do you do?

retell every detail in the exact order
retell only the most important ideas in a few sentences
explain whether you liked the story
explanation: A summary briefly states the main ideas and key events without all the small details or your opinions.

stem: Read the sentence: "The scientist repeated the test three times to CONFIRM her results." What does CONFIRM mean?
explanation: Repeating a test helps a scientist make sure the results are correct. Confirm means to show or make sure that something is true.

stem: The recipe says to PREHEAT the oven. What does PREHEAT mean?
explanation: The prefix pre- means 'before.' To preheat the oven is to heat it before putting the food in.

stem:

After Lily has finished her homework, she went outside to play.
After Lily will have finished her homework, she went outside to play.
After Lily had finish her homework, she went outside to play.
explanation: The past perfect is formed with 'had' plus the past participle ('had finished'). It shows that finishing homework happened before going outside.

Yesterday Omar walked to the park and plays soccer with his cousins.
Tomorrow Omar will walk to the park and play soccer with his cousins.
Yesterday Omar walked to the park and played soccer with his cousins.
explanation: 'Yesterday' tells us the actions happened in the past, so both verbs should be past tense. 'Walked' is past, but 'plays' shifts to present tense for no reason.

explanation: With 'neither...nor,' the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. 'Teacher' is singular, so the verb is 'was.'

explanation: With 'either...or,' the verb agrees with the closer subject. 'Mother' is singular, so the verb is 'is.'

After the long hike we, rested beside the stream.
After the long hike, we rested beside the stream.
After, the long hike we rested beside the stream.
explanation: The introductory phrase is 'After the long hike.' The comma belongs right after the whole phrase, before the main clause 'we rested beside the stream.'

Yes, I would love to come to your party.
Yes I would love to come, to your party.
Yes I, would love to come to your party.
explanation: A comma is used to set off the word 'yes' or 'no' at the beginning of a sentence.

You finished your science, project didn't you?

You finished your science project didn't, you?
explanation: A tag question such as 'didn't you?' at the end of a sentence is set off with a comma.

Thank you Ms., Rivera for helping us with the play.
explanation: When a name in direct address comes in the middle of a sentence, commas go both before and after it.

Our class sang "This Land Is Your Land" at the assembly.
explanation: Titles of short works such as songs, poems, and short stories are placed in quotation marks. The quotation marks must surround the whole title and only the title.

"The kite drifted above the tall trees."

"The library is ______ the bakery and the post office."
explanation: 'Between' is used to show a position in the middle of two things: the bakery and the post office. 'Among' is used for three or more.

explanation: 'News' ends in -s but is a singular noun. The singular verb 'is' agrees with it.

stem:
